q: State one role of dopamine in the brain.

pts.a: It gives a feeling of pleasure (reward) that motivates us to repeat a behaviour
accept: it is the brain's reward chemical
it motivates you to do things again

pts.a: It helps to control movement (too little causes Parkinson's disease)
accept: it is needed for smooth movements

right: It gives a feeling of pleasure (reward) that motivates behaviour
wrong: It breaks down other neurotransmitters in the cleft
It insulates axons so impulses travel faster
It carries oxygen to the brain cells
why: Dopamine is the brain's reward neurotransmitter: it gives a feeling of pleasure that motivates us to repeat a behaviour. It also helps to control movement.

q: State one role of endorphins in the body.

pts.a: They relieve pain: they are the body's natural painkillers
They give a feeling of well-being (euphoria), for example after exercise
accept: they give a feeling of well-being

right: They act as natural painkillers, blocking pain
wrong: They control the heartbeat and breathing
They make the myelin sheath
They speed up digestion
why: Endorphins are neurotransmitters released during stress, pain and exercise: they block pain signals and give a feeling of well-being (the 'runner's high').

q: Explain how regular exercise can affect a person's mood.

pts.a: Exercise causes the release of endorphins (and dopamine)
These lift mood: a feeling of well-being, with less pain and stress
accept: it gives a feeling of well-being

right: It releases endorphins, which give a feeling of well-being
wrong: It lowers dopamine, so you feel flat afterwards
It uses up the endorphins, so mood gets worse
It stops the brain making any neurotransmitters
why: Exercise triggers the release of endorphins (and dopamine). Endorphins reduce pain and stress and give a feeling of well-being, so mood improves.

q: Some drugs, such as cocaine, raise dopamine levels at synapses. Suggest why such drugs can become addictive.

pts.a: The extra dopamine gives an intense feeling of pleasure (reward)
accept: they give a strong feeling of pleasure

pts.a: The brain adapts (fewer receptors, less dopamine made), so more of the drug is needed and the user craves it
accept: more of the drug is needed each time

right: They give intense pleasure, and the brain adapts so more is needed
wrong: They block dopamine, so the user feels pain
They destroy the myelin sheath of the axons
They lower dopamine, giving a calm, sleepy feeling
why: Drugs that flood synapses with dopamine give an intense feeling of pleasure (reward). The brain adapts, for example by making fewer receptors, so more drug is needed and the user craves it.

q: Suggest how a person's diet can affect their dopamine levels.

pts.a: Sugary or fatty foods trigger a release of dopamine (a reward), so they can be craved
accept: junk food gives a burst of dopamine

pts.a: Dopamine is made from an amino acid (tyrosine) found in protein foods
accept: dopamine is made from amino acids

right: Sugary, fatty foods trigger a burst of dopamine, a reward feeling
wrong: Eating vitamin C destroys dopamine in the brain
Drinking water turns dopamine into endorphins
Fibre in the diet blocks every dopamine receptor
why: Sugary and fatty foods trigger a release of dopamine (a reward), which is why they can be craved; dopamine itself is made from tyrosine, an amino acid in protein foods.

q: Some drugs inhibit the enzyme that breaks down a neurotransmitter. Explain the effect this has at the synapse.

pts.a: The neurotransmitter is not broken down, so it stays in the cleft longer (builds up)
accept: it stays in the cleft for longer

pts.a: It keeps binding to the receptors, so the next neuron is stimulated more: an enhanced effect

right: It stays in the cleft longer, so its effect on the next neuron is enhanced
wrong: It is broken down faster, so the impulse is weaker
It can no longer be released from the vesicles
It is carried away in the blood to the kidneys
why: With the enzyme blocked the neurotransmitter isn't broken down: it stays in the cleft and keeps binding to receptors, so the next neuron is stimulated more (an enhanced effect).

q: Some antidepressant drugs are reuptake inhibitors. Explain what a reuptake inhibitor does at a synapse.

pts.a: It stops the presynaptic neuron taking the neurotransmitter back in (reabsorbing it)
accept: it stops the neurotransmitter being reabsorbed
it prevents the neuron taking it back in

pts.a: So more neurotransmitter stays in the cleft for longer: an enhanced effect (e.g. a raised mood)
accept: it lasts longer in the cleft

right: It stops the neuron reabsorbing the transmitter, so more stays in the cleft
wrong: It breaks the neurotransmitter down faster
It stops vesicles releasing the neurotransmitter
It blocks the receptors so no impulse is made
why: Normally the presynaptic neuron reabsorbs the neurotransmitter. A reuptake inhibitor blocks this, so more stays in the cleft for longer and its effect is enhanced.

q: Painkillers such as morphine act at synapses in the pain pathways. Suggest how a painkiller could reduce the feeling of pain.

pts.a: It blocks transmission of impulses across synapses in the pain pathway, so fewer impulses reach the brain
accept: it stops impulses crossing the synapse

pts.a: It mimics endorphins, binding to their receptors

right: It blocks impulses crossing the synapses, so fewer reach the brain
wrong: It speeds up impulses so the pain passes quickly
It heals the damaged tissue straight away
It makes extra receptors for pain signals
why: Painkillers such as morphine block transmission at synapses in the pain pathways, partly by mimicking endorphins, so fewer impulses reach the brain and less pain is felt.

q: Psychoactive drugs change mood and behaviour. Give one way in which such a drug can act at a synapse.

pts.a: It mimics a neurotransmitter and binds to its receptors
accept: it binds to the receptors instead

pts.a: It blocks the receptors so the neurotransmitter cannot bind
It stops the neurotransmitter being broken down or reabsorbed, so more stays in the cleft
It makes more neurotransmitter be released
accept: it increases the release of neurotransmitter

right: It mimics a neurotransmitter and binds to its receptors
wrong: It destroys the myelin sheath
It replaces the cell body of the neuron
It travels along the axon instead of the impulse
why: A psychoactive drug can mimic a neurotransmitter, block its receptors, stop its breakdown or reuptake, or boost its release, changing transmission and so mood.

q: Disruptions to synaptic transmission can cause acute or chronic disorders. Distinguish between an acute and a chronic disorder.

pts.a: An acute disorder comes on suddenly and is short-lived
A chronic disorder develops slowly and lasts a long time
accept: chronic disorders last a long time

right: An acute disorder starts suddenly; a chronic one lasts a long time
wrong: An acute disorder lasts a long time; a chronic one starts suddenly
Acute disorders are caused by germs; chronic ones by genes
Both are short-lived, but chronic ones are painful
why: An acute disorder comes on suddenly and is short-lived; a chronic disorder develops slowly and lasts a long time, like Parkinson's disease.

q: Parkinson's disease is a chronic disorder in which the neurons that release dopamine die. Explain why a drug that stops dopamine being broken down can help.

pts.a: Less dopamine is broken down, so more stays at the synapses (its level rises)
accept: more dopamine stays at the synapse

pts.a: So transmission is enhanced and movement improves (fewer symptoms)

right: More dopamine stays at the synapses, so movement improves
wrong: It kills the remaining dopamine neurons faster
It makes the brain stop needing dopamine
It raises dopamine in the blood so it reaches the bones
why: If dopamine isn't broken down, more of the little that is released stays at the synapses and keeps stimulating receptors, enhancing transmission so movement improves.

q: Depression is linked to low levels of the neurotransmitter serotonin at synapses. Suggest how a drug could relieve depression.

pts.a: It stops serotonin being reabsorbed (a reuptake inhibitor) or broken down, so more stays in the cleft
accept: it blocks the reuptake of serotonin
it raises serotonin levels at the synapse

right: It stops serotonin being reabsorbed, so more stays in the cleft
wrong: It blocks the serotonin receptors
It speeds up the breakdown of serotonin
It lowers the amount of serotonin released
why: Low serotonin is linked to depression. A reuptake inhibitor stops the presynaptic neuron reabsorbing it, so more stays in the cleft and its effect on mood is enhanced.

q: What is meant by negative feedback in homeostasis?

pts.a: A change from the normal level sets off a response that reverses the change, bringing it back to normal
accept: it brings conditions back to normal

right: A change sets off a response that reverses it, back to normal
wrong: A change sets off a response that makes it even bigger
The brain ignores small changes in the body
A hormone is released and never switched off
why: In negative feedback a change away from the normal level is detected and the response reverses it, bringing conditions back to normal.

q: Homeostasis works as a stimulus-response system. State the role of the receptor and of the effector.

pts.a: The receptor detects the change (the stimulus)
accept: the receptor picks up the change

pts.a: The effector carries out the response that corrects it
accept: effectors respond to correct the change

right: The receptor detects the change; the effector carries out the response
wrong: The effector detects the change; the receptor carries out the response
Both detect the change and send it into the blood
The receptor stores the change; the effector forgets it
why: Receptors detect a change (the stimulus); the control centre in the brain processes it; effectors (muscles or glands) carry out the response that corrects it.

q: Name the two pathways that link the control centre with the receptors and effectors in homeostasis.

pts.a: The nervous pathway (nerves)
The hormonal pathway (hormones in the blood)

right: The nervous pathway and the hormonal pathway
wrong: The nervous and the lymphatic pathways
The digestive and the respiratory pathways
The blood and the lymph pathways
why: The control centre is linked to receptors and effectors by nerves (the nervous pathway, fast) and by hormones carried in the blood (the hormonal pathway, slower).

q: In negative feedback, explain why the response must stop once conditions are back to normal.

pts.a: Otherwise the level would overshoot and go too far the other way
accept: it would go too far the other way
the level would become too low or too high

right: Otherwise it would overshoot, going too far the other way
wrong: So that the receptors can grow back
Because effectors can only work once
So the hormone can be stored in the brain
why: Negative feedback switches the response off once the level is back to normal; if it carried on, the level would overshoot and go too far the other way.

q: Where are the cell bodies of sensory neurons found, just outside the spinal cord?

pts.a: In a ganglion (swelling) on the dorsal root
accept: in a swelling on the dorsal root

right: In a ganglion (a swelling) on the dorsal root
wrong: In the white matter of the cord
In the effector muscle
In the meninges around the cord
why: Sensory neurons enter the cord by the dorsal (back) root; their cell bodies sit in a swelling on it, the dorsal root ganglion. Motor cell bodies are in the grey matter.

q: A spinal nerve contains sensory and motor fibres. Through which root does each type enter or leave the spinal cord?

pts.a: Sensory fibres enter through the dorsal (back) root
accept: sensory neurons come in at the back
sensory fibres use the dorsal root

pts.a: Motor fibres leave through the ventral (front) root
accept: motor neurons leave at the front
motor fibres use the ventral root

right: Sensory fibres enter by the dorsal root; motor fibres leave by the ventral root
wrong: Sensory fibres enter by the ventral root; motor fibres leave by the dorsal root
Both enter and leave by the dorsal root
Both pass in and out through the central canal
why: Sensory fibres enter the spinal cord through the dorsal (back) root, which has a ganglion; motor fibres leave through the ventral (front) root. The two roots join to form a spinal nerve.

q: In which region of the spinal cord are the cell bodies of motor neurons and interneurons found?

pts.a: In the grey matter

right: In the grey matter, the butterfly-shaped core
wrong: In the white matter
In the dorsal root ganglion
In the central canal
why: Motor neuron and interneuron cell bodies are in the grey matter of the cord; the white matter is axons, and sensory cell bodies sit in the dorsal root ganglion outside it.

q: A student models a synapse with two people passing a ball across a gap. In the model, what does the ball stand for, and what does the gap stand for?

pts.a: The ball is the neurotransmitter
accept: the ball is the chemical messenger

pts.a: The gap is the synaptic cleft
accept: the gap stands for the synaptic cleft

right: The ball is the neurotransmitter; the gap is the synaptic cleft
wrong: The ball is the synaptic cleft; the gap is the neurotransmitter
The ball is the impulse; the gap is the axon
The ball is the myelin; the gap is the vesicle
why: In the model the ball is the neurotransmitter and the gap is the synaptic cleft: the electrical impulse can't jump the gap, so a chemical carries the message across.

q: In a model of a synapse, why should the ball only ever be passed from the first person to the second, and never back?

pts.a: Only the presynaptic neuron has vesicles to release neurotransmitter, and only the postsynaptic one has receptors, so impulses cross one way
accept: only the first neuron has vesicles
only the second neuron has receptors
impulses only cross a synapse one way

right: Only the first neuron has vesicles; only the second has receptors
wrong: The ball is too heavy to pass back
The gap gets wider after each pass
Neurotransmitter is destroyed by the myelin
why: Vesicles are only in the presynaptic neuron and receptors only on the postsynaptic one, so a synapse passes impulses in one direction; the model should too.

q: In the model, the second person catches the ball and then drops it into a bin. What does dropping the ball into the bin represent?

pts.a: The neurotransmitter being broken down by an enzyme (or reabsorbed), so it stops stimulating the next neuron
accept: it is broken down by an enzyme

right: An enzyme breaking the neurotransmitter down after it has worked
wrong: The impulse being released from the vesicles
The neurotransmitter crossing the cleft
The neurotransmitter binding to the receptors
why: Once it has passed on the impulse the neurotransmitter is broken down by an enzyme (or reabsorbed); otherwise the next neuron would keep firing. The bin stands for that.
